contributions.text: To ask His Majesty’s Government what assessment they have made of the effectiveness of prison education and employment programmes in reducing reoffending.
contributions.name: Baroness Prentis of Banbury

contributions.who: Baroness in Waiting/Government Whip (Baroness Hyde of Bemerton) (Lab)
contributions.text: Education and employment are vital to rehabilitation, each reducing reoffending by up to nine percentage points. Prison education, together with other work-focused activities, builds skills for life including reading, numeracy and work-focused training. Employment partnerships and employer-led skills training programmes develop the skills needed for sustainable work on release. The Government are undertaking a full evaluation of a new prisoner education service and continue to monitor delivery outcomes across education, skills and employment provision to inform future development.
contributions.name: Baroness Hyde of Bemerton

contributions.text: I think the whole House will agree with the tenor of what the noble Baroness has just told us. Will she reassure us that she will do everything she can to reduce friction in accessing education in our overcrowded prisons? One specific example is removing the need for teachers to do a key training programme for each individual establishment rather than one for everywhere.
contributions.name: Baroness Prentis of Banbury

contributions.text: I am unsure whether the noble and learned Baroness refers to keys that lock and unlock, or key as in core.
contributions.name: Baroness Hyde of Bemerton

contributions.text: Core.
contributions.name: Baroness Prentis of Banbury

contributions.text: I thank her for that clarification. I will take the query about the core training provision back to the team, because we are absolutely committed and focused on the need to be able to access consistent education. This Government seek to smooth the way so that teachers can be in classrooms teaching prisoners who are able to get the skills they need before they leave prison.
contributions.name: Baroness Hyde of Bemerton

contributions.text: My Lords, I am delighted that the Prime Minister is providing leadership and funding on rough sleeping. Prisoners have a far higher rate of reoffending when they leave prison and find themselves homeless. What action are the Government taking to deal with homelessness among prison leavers?
contributions.name: Baroness Brown of Silvertown

contributions.text: I thank the noble Baroness for that question. As noble Lords may be aware, some time ago, prior to coming to this place, I sat in many homeless persons units—with prisoners on the day of release in different local authorities across London —trying to enable people to access accommodation. It is a personal passion of mine. Stable accommodation, as the noble Baroness says, is fundamental to successful rehabilitation and reducing reoffending, because those who are homeless on release have reoffending rates around double those released into settled accommodation. Through the national plan to end homelessness, the Government have committed to halving the proportion of prison leavers released homeless and increasing the proportion in settled accommodation three months after release by the end of this Parliament. As the noble Baroness rightly says, the Prime Minister’s rough sleeping programme is backed by £874 million, which builds on that national plan, taking the total homelessness investment to over £4 billion over the next three years.
contributions.name: Baroness Hyde of Bemerton

contributions.text: My Lords, Highpoint prison in Newmarket does amazing work equipping prisoners with CSCS and CPCS cards so that they can go straight on to building sites. On a recent visit, the prison told me and other noble Lords that changes in funding were making it increasingly difficult to provide that specific form of training. Will the Government look at this explicitly in monitoring what is happening? If possible, can the Minister inform the House or me whether anything is being done to address these problems?
contributions.name: Baroness Wolf of Dulwich

contributions.text: I am unaware of the specific details around the case mentioned in HMP Highpoint, but I take the point that CSCS cards are an incredibly important progression route for many people who are currently incarcerated. As I am sure the noble Baroness is aware, governors have localised commissioning powers so that they can commission specialist provision in terms of local education assessed against labour market needs. The Government are expanding provision to vocational training, prison industries and work-based learning so that people can secure employment on release. One example is through the future skills programme, which aligns training with employer demand and includes a guaranteed interview before release. I will happily write to the noble Baroness about that specific prison.
contributions.name: Baroness Hyde of Bemerton

contributions.text: My Lords, reoffending costs £22.7 billion a year. Reducing reoffending means increasing the level of education and training in our prisons, not cutting it as is currently happening. Is the Minister aware that the Chancellor has announced plans for a preventive departmental expenditure limit, which is ring-fenced funding to fix problems and bring down costs in the future? Is her department at least looking at that as a mechanism to dig itself out of the hole that it has created?
contributions.name: Lord Foster of Bath

contributions.text: The noble Lord will be unsurprised to hear that, given our dedication to this agenda, we are absolutely looking at pulling every single lever to ensure that people leave prisons with a high level of education and skills that will enable them to get into work or further training when they leave prison.
contributions.name: Baroness Hyde of Bemerton

contributions.text: My Lords, prisoners are being released so quickly by this Government that it is difficult to believe that many of them have time for either education or employment—and, of course, many of them quickly return. The quarterly recall figures for April to June 2026 show a 12% increase from the same quarter a year earlier. It is acknowledged that this is in part due to what has been termed by the Prime Minister “the early release scheme”. Will the Minister ensure that, when the reoffending data for the same period is released, it is broken down to identify the number of prisoners who had been released early?
contributions.name: Lord Keen of Elie

contributions.text: We recognise the issue of recall. It serves nobody if people are going into prison on very short sentences and then coming out. That is why we progressed the Sentencing Act through the other House and this House; it has gone on to statute and become law. There may be some learning-curve amendments from that, but fundamentally we are having to address the overcrowding crisis through the provisions of the Sentencing Act and using this progressive route to enable people to resettle into crime-free lives, of which education and employment—as we have already alluded to—are a key part.
contributions.name: Baroness Hyde of Bemerton

contributions.text: My Lords, as chair of the Prison Reform Trust, I can say that there is strong evidence of education and training in prison being an investment in life chances and a safer society. Although the ink is barely dry on Alan Milburn’s report, will my noble friend the Minister look at extending the proposed opportunity support guarantee—a route into education, training or work—to young people in prison?
contributions.name: Lord Stace

contributions.text: I thank the noble Lord for all his excellent work in this arena and with the Prison Reform Trust. I know he is aware that, at present, prisons work hard to ensure that young people can access a broad range of educational opportunities including functional skills, vocational training, distance learning and work experience. Every prisoner receives an education assessment and careers guidance, which informs digital work, and a learning plan that supports progression throughout their time in custody. I welcome Alan Milburn’s ambition to increase apprenticeship opportunities for young people. HMPPS is already working with employers to expand apprenticeship provision in custody, including in sectors such as construction and hospitality, helping prisoners develop the skills they need for successful employment on release.
contributions.name: Baroness Hyde of Bemerton

contributions.text: My Lords, many prisoners go into prison addicted, and many prisoners get addicted while in prison. The previous holder of the Minister’s post assured me that, by the end of this year, every prison in England would have AA and Narcotics Anonymous. Tomorrow is our annual fundraiser for the Rehabilitation for Addicted Prisoners Trust. Can I please tell the fundraiser that this pledge is being fulfilled?
contributions.name: Baroness Boycott

contributions.text: The noble Baroness will be unsurprised that I will need to confirm that and write to her as I do not have it in my pack. I take the opportunity to thank NA and AA for their work. Having worked in prisons for over a decade, I recognise their essential work. This Government have invested over £300 million in trying to keep prisons safe and secure. A core part of that—£75 million—has been invested in improving physical security so that we can tackle drugs and other contraband coming in, as well as increasing access to mutual aid across the estate. We are working closely with the fellowship organisations that the noble Baroness mentioned.
contributions.name: Baroness Hyde of Bemerton

contributions.text: My Lords, does the Minister agree that the prison library system is central to education in prisons, and that the library system is not always as accessible as it should be because there is a shortage of trained librarians? I declare an interest in that my wife is a trustee of a prison reading group charity.
contributions.name: Lord Waldegrave of North Hill

contributions.text: I agree with the noble Lord that libraries are essential. In my time working in prisons, I remember being shocked the first time I heard the statistic that the average reading age for a prisoner is 11 years old. I pay tribute to the work of organisations such as the Shannon Trust, which are vital in ensuring that, beyond the higher education opportunities, basic numeracy and literacy are widely accessible within all our prisons.
contributions.name: Baroness Hyde of Bemerton

contributions.text: My Lords, it is estimated that 25% to 40% of care leavers end up in prison, and it is higher—about 50%—for children in custody. Most of those have underachieved in education. What programmes are there specifically to address this?
contributions.name: Baroness Hussein-Ece

contributions.text: The noble Baroness is right to raise the overrepresentation of care leavers, particularly in the women’s estate and the youth estate. We are committed to tackling that problem. We recognise the importance of early intervention and prevention across a range of things, particularly so that it is not inevitable that a child leaving care will end up in the criminal justice system. We are committed to ending that pipeline.
contributions.name: Baroness Hyde of Bemerton
